case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) permits a damages suit against the United States Postal Service for the alleged intentional, discriminatory loss/deprivation of a postal customer’s property, or whether an FTCA exception bars the claim and leaves the plaintiff without a remedy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680 (including the FTCA’s exceptions, especially the ‘postal matter’/‘loss of mail’ exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b)); relatedly, the Westfall Act substitution/exclusivity provisions, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b), as they affect whether plaintiffs can sue individual federal employees when FTCA relief is unavailable.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: USPS and the United States argue that respondent’s claim is barred by an FTCA exception—most directly § 2680(b), which withholds the FTCA waiver for claims arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter—because the harm alleged (missing or mishandled mail/property connected to postal delivery) fits within that exception. Petitioners’ practical bottom line is that Congress preserved sovereign immunity for these mail-loss-type claims, and courts should not narrow the exception by recharacterizing the claim as intentional discrimination or other wrongdoing when the injury still ‘arises out of’ loss/mishandling of postal matter. Petitioners also lean on the broader remedial structure after the Westfall Act and the Court’s restrictive approach to implied constitutional remedies (Bivens), emphasizing that the judiciary should not expand liability beyond the limits Congress set in the FTCA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Konan argues that her suit does not fall within § 2680(b) because it is not a classic ‘lost mail’ claim about routine transmission failures; rather, it involves intentional, discriminatory, and/or ultra vires conduct by postal employees resulting in a property deprivation. She contends the Fifth Circuit correctly treated the FTCA as providing the available remedy in a remedial landscape where Bivens is rarely extended and the Westfall Act often forecloses state-law claims against individual officials. Respondent and supporting amici maintain that petitioners’ reading would improperly enlarge the exception to swallow the FTCA’s waiver whenever postal employees’ misconduct can be described as ‘loss of postal matter,’ effectively placing federal officials above ordinary tort accountability and undermining the FTCA’s role as a core substitute remedy.
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: Dolan cautioned that §2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities,” and they argue intentional, discriminatory deprivation is not the sort of “loss” Congress had in mind. But the text Congress enacted is not motive-based; it withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of … postal matter,” and the injury alleged here—nonreceipt/deprivation of mailed items—still arises out of a mail-loss event as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize. Dolan’s limiting principle turns on the type of harm (injuries attributable to mail failing to arrive, versus independent torts like slip-and-fall), not on whether the failure was negligent or intentional. However serious the remedial gap, we cannot create an intent-based carveout from a retained-immunity provision without a clear textual hook.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly emphasize Dolan’s caution that § 2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities,” and they would confine the exception to routine transmission failures rather than intentional discrimination. But Congress barred “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of … postal matter,” and respondent’s claimed injury—nonreceipt/deprivation of mailed items—still arises from a failure of postal matter to reach its destination, whatever motive is alleged. As the Chief Justice notes, we may not enlarge the FTCA’s waiver by pleading labels or remedial-gap concerns; once § 2680(b) applies, sovereign immunity remains and the court lacks jurisdiction. Any resulting remedial consequences from the Westfall Act’s allocation of suits and the limited availability of Bivens are for Congress to address, not for us to cure by adding an intent-based carveout not found in the text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best case that Dolan cautioned § 2680(b) does not "immunize all postal activities" and that "loss" should not be read to cover intentional, discriminatory interference. But the enacted text withdraws the waiver for "[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage" of "postal matter," and—as the Chief Justice notes—the gravamen here is still nonreceipt/deprivation of mail, i.e., harm flowing from postal matter that failed to arrive as intended. Dolan’s line-drawing turns on the type of injury (mail failing to arrive, arriving damaged, late, or at the wrong place), not on the alleged mental state of the employee, and nothing in § 2680(b)’s grammar supplies an intent-based carveout that would restore jurisdiction. The remedial gap Sotomayor identifies is a consequence of Congress’s chosen limits on the FTCA waiver (and the Westfall Act’s channeling), not a warrant for us to narrow a retained-immunity provision beyond its ordinary meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that “arising out of” is broad and that we may not create an atextual intent-based carveout from § 2680(b). But Dolan’s instruction that § 2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities” is not satisfied merely by pointing to slip-and-fall cases; it speaks to the exception’s historical office—shielding the Government from ordinary transmission failures (mail lost, delayed, damaged, or misdelivered), not from alleged intentional, discriminatory interference with property that is ultra vires in kind. Reading “loss” to encompass any intentional deprivation would give Congress’s targeted postal-matter exception a sweeping operation that threatens to nullify the FTCA’s remedial aim for a category of wrongful conduct that the Westfall Act channels into the FTCA with no clear alternative damages remedy. Because sovereign immunity waivers must be strictly construed but statutory amendments and line-drawing must also have “real and substantial effect,” I would construe § 2680(b) consistent with its transmission-failure focus and allow the claim to proceed past the exception stage.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best push by invoking Dolan’s warning that §2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities” and by recasting this as intentional, discriminatory interference rather than a transmission failure. But §2680(b)’s text withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of postal matter, and this plaintiff’s damages theory still turns on nonreceipt/deprivation of mailed items—harm that flows from a mail-loss event. As the Chief Justice notes, nothing in the statutory grammar creates an intent-based carveout, and creating one would add an atextual exception-to-the-exception contrary to the FTCA’s rule/exception structure and clear-statement discipline for waivers. Dolan’s limitation is satisfied by keeping outside §2680(b) injuries not attributable to missing mail (e.g., slip-and-fall), while leaving mail-loss injuries—however alleged motive—within the retained immunity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson fairly invoke Dolan’s caution that § 2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities,” urging a narrowing to routine transmission failures and excluding intentional, discriminatory deprivation. But the text Congress enacted withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of … postal matter,” and the claimed injury here—nonreceipt/deprivation of mail—still “arises out of” a loss/miscarriage event, whatever the alleged motive; as the Chief Justice notes, pleading labels cannot rewrite the operative causal link Congress described. Dolan’s line is best understood as distinguishing mail-loss harms (immune) from other harms incident to postal operations (not immune), not as silently creating an intent-based carveout Congress did not write. Because § 2680(b) independently restores immunity, I would not proceed to the FTCA’s private-analog merits inquiry or attempt to cure any remedial gap through atextual narrowing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: Dolan warns that § 2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities,” and they would confine the exception to routine transmission failures rather than intentional, discriminatory deprivation. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, the enacted text withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of … postal matter,” and the injury alleged here is still nonreceipt/deprivation of mail—harm that flows from postal matter failing to arrive as intended—regardless of the employee’s motive. Dolan’s limiting principle is satisfied by keeping non-mail-loss injuries (like slip-and-fall hazards from delivery) outside the exception, while maintaining immunity for claims whose gravamen is missing or misdelivered mail. The remedial-gap concern is real, but it cannot supply a waiver Congress did not unmistakably provide, especially given the FTCA’s structure of a waiver “subject to” enumerated exceptions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make their best point by invoking Dolan’s warning that §2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities,” and by stressing the troubling remedial gap if intentional discriminatory interference is swept in. But the statutory text withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of “postal matter,” and—as the Chief Justice explains—the gravamen here is still nonreceipt/deprivation of mail because it failed to arrive as intended; motive does not change what the claim “arises out of.” Dolan’s limiting principle turns on the type of injury (mail-loss versus independent tort injuries like slip-and-fall), not on an intent-based carveout that Congress did not write. Whatever policy concerns follow from Westfall Act exclusivity and limited Bivens availability cannot justify narrowing a retained-immunity provision beyond its ordinary meaning.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that a claim for nonreceipt of mail will often “aris[e] out of” a mail-loss event regardless of how the plaintiff pleads motive, and I agree courts cannot manufacture waivers Congress did not provide. But § 2680(b)’s text and operation within the FTCA still matter: Congress excepted claims arising out of “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission,” and—read structurally, and consistent with Dolan’s insistence that the provision does not “immunize all postal activities”—those terms most naturally track breakdowns in the process of transmission and delivery, not an alleged intentional, discriminatory confiscation that is the gravamen of this suit. Treating any intentional deprivation as a “loss” risks converting a targeted transmission carveout into a broad immunity for wrongful interference with property under color of postal employment, a scope expansion the statutory words do not compel. I therefore would confine § 2680(b) to transmission failures (including negligent misdelivery and ordinary loss) and leave the FTCA waiver in place for the intentional discriminatory seizure claim as pleaded.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity applies only "subject to" the exceptions in § 2680, and § 2680(b) withdraws that waiver for "[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage" of "postal matter." On the facts alleged, respondent’s injury is the deprivation of her mailed property—i.e., harm that flows directly from mail failing to be delivered as intended—and relabeling the employees’ conduct as intentional or discriminatory does not change that the claim still "arises out of" a mail-loss event covered by the exception. Consistent with a notice/traditional-remedies baseline, Congress preserved immunity for this category of claims and provided alternative, more limited administrative/insurance remedies; courts are not free to expand damages exposure beyond the textually retained immunity merely because other remedial paths (including Bivens) are narrow. The statute’s language must be applied coherently across theories of wrongdoing: if the loss-of-mail exception bars negligence-based mail-loss claims, the same operative event cannot be transformed into an FTCA claim simply by adding intent-based descriptors while seeking the same damages for the same missing postal matter.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver extends only to claims “actionable under § 1346(b),” and Congress expressly withdrew that waiver in § 2680(b) for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Respondent’s alleged injury is the nonreceipt/deprivation of her mail and related property because USPS employees allegedly refused to deliver it, which fits squarely within the exception’s text because the claim still “aris[es] out of” lost or miscarried postal matter regardless of the employees’ asserted motive. Because an FTCA exception applies, sovereign immunity remains, and neither courts nor equitable concerns about remedial gaps permit expanding the waiver beyond Congress’s specified terms. To the extent respondent argues the Westfall Act otherwise leaves her without a damages remedy against individual employees, that is a consequence of Congress’s remedial-allocation scheme and does not alter the FTCA’s jurisdictional limits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by the exceptions Congress enacted, and § 2680(b) withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of “postal matter.” On the alleged facts, respondent’s injury is the nonreceipt/deprivation of mail or mail-related property—i.e., harm that arises directly from postal matter failing to arrive—so the claim falls within the exception even if respondent characterizes the underlying conduct as intentional or discriminatory. Dolan makes clear that § 2680(b) generally preserves immunity for injuries attributable to mail that “fails to arrive at all” or arrives in the wrong condition or place, and courts are not free to narrow that textual bar to preserve a damages remedy. If the upshot is that respondent is left without an FTCA remedy (and the Westfall Act/Bivens doctrine offers no substitute), that is a consequence of the remedial limits Congress chose, not a gap for the judiciary to fill.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The United States is immune absent an unequivocal waiver, but courts must also give Congress’s waivers and amendments “real and substantial effect” and avoid reading exceptions so broadly that they nullify the FTCA’s remedial role for ordinary tort wrongs. Section 2680(b), as construed in Dolan, preserves immunity for injuries arising because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or misdelivered—i.e., transmission failures—yet it does not “immunize all postal activities,” and respondent alleges intentional, discriminatory deprivation of her property rather than a routine loss or negligent transmission. Applying the exception’s purpose and historical backdrop, extending § 2680(b) to intentional, ultra vires discrimination would convert a targeted mail-loss carveout into a sweeping shield for unconstitutional or invidious misconduct, leaving plaintiffs without any meaningful substitute remedy in light of Westfall Act exclusivity and the Court’s narrow Bivens doctrine. Because the gravamen here is intentional discriminatory wrongdoing—not the sort of policy-laden judgment the FTCA’s exceptions are designed to protect—the claim should proceed within the FTCA’s waiver rather than be categorically barred by § 2680(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited, text-defined waiver of sovereign immunity, and the plaintiff bears the burden to show her claim fits within §1346(b)’s grant rather than an enumerated exception in §2680. On these facts, the injury she seeks to redress is the non-delivery/deprivation of items that were “letters or postal matter,” so her damages claim “aris[es] out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of mail within §2680(b) as Dolan describes—covering harms that occur because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or at the wrong address. Recasting the same core harm as intentional or discriminatory misconduct does not supply the clear statutory basis needed to overcome Congress’s retained immunity in the postal-matter exception; Congress drew that carve-out, and courts may not narrow it by pleading labels. Whatever the remedial gap created by Westfall Act exclusivity and the Court’s restrained approach to implied constitutional remedies, that policy concern cannot substitute for the unmistakably clear waiver Congress did not provide for mail-loss claims.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver for “injury or loss of property” in § 1346(b)(1) applies only subject to § 2680’s textually enumerated exceptions, each of which independently withdraws the waiver. Here, the gravamen of respondent’s complaint is that her property/mail went missing or was not delivered in the course of postal operations, so her damages claim “aris[es] out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of … postal matter” and falls within § 2680(b)’s carveout, leaving sovereign immunity intact even if the alleged loss was intentional or discriminatory. Nothing in § 2680’s structure suggests we may narrow subsection (b) by importing limitations from elsewhere; and once the exception applies, we do not reach the FTCA merits inquiry about “private individual under like circumstances” liability under state law. That Congress’s remedial scheme (including Westfall Act exclusivity and the Court’s reluctance to extend Bivens) may leave this plaintiff without a damages remedy is a policy consequence the statute’s text assigns to Congress, not the courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by the exceptions Congress expressly retained, and § 2680(b) withdraws the waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Here, the concrete injury alleged is the non-delivery/deprivation of postal matter or property connected to mail delivery, and—even if the plaintiff characterizes the underlying conduct as intentional or discriminatory—the claim still “arises out of” a loss or miscarriage of postal matter within the statutory text and structure Congress enacted. Dolan confirms that § 2680(b) preserves immunity for harms stemming from mail that “fails to arrive at all” or is mishandled, and courts should not evade that line by re-labeling a mail-loss claim as a different tort when the gravamen remains missing/misdelivered mail. Because Congress has not clearly authorized an FTCA damages remedy for this category of mail-loss injury, the judicial role is to apply the retained immunity as written, even if that leaves respondent without an FTCA remedy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver is limited by § 2680(b), which withdraws jurisdiction for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of postal matter; read in ordinary usage and in context, respondent’s alleged injury—nonreceipt/deprivation of mailed property traceable to postal handling—still “arises out of” the loss or miscarriage of mail even if she characterizes the employees’ conduct as intentional or discriminatory. Dolan’s construction of § 2680(b) focuses on the type of harm (mail that fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or misdelivered), and this case fits that category because the gravamen is a delivery failure resulting in missing property. The statute’s structure also counsels against carving out an intent-based exception that Congress did not write, especially given that FTCA exceptions are part of the sovereign-immunity baseline and courts may not expand the waiver by relabeling the theory of wrongdoing while the injury remains mail-loss-related. That outcome may leave respondent without an FTCA damages remedy, but the remedial gap is for Congress to address; the text of § 2680(b) controls.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FTCA’s text waives sovereign immunity for “negligent or wrongful” acts by federal employees, and § 2680(b) withdraws that waiver only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of postal matter. Reading that exception in light of its structure and operation within the FTCA—and consistent with Dolan’s instruction that § 2680(b) does not “immunize all postal activities”—the best reading is that Congress carved out routine delivery failures (mail that fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or misdelivered), not an alleged intentional, discriminatory deprivation of a customer’s property by postal employees. Treating intentional, discriminatory confiscation as categorically “loss” would expand the exception beyond its terms and collapse the FTCA’s remedial design in precisely the setting where other avenues (e.g., Bivens, state-law employee suits post-Westfall Act) are often unavailable. On these facts, the claim targets wrongful intentional misconduct rather than a transmission failure, so § 2680(b) should not bar the suit.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) permits a damages suit against the United States/USPS for alleged intentional misconduct by postal employees, or whether one or more FTCA exceptions strip federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction over the claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680), including FTCA exceptions (28 U.S.C. § 2680) and the Westfall Act’s substitution/exclusivity rules (28 U.S.C. § 2679); with background reliance on remedial/constitutional-accountability considerations (including 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(2)(A) referencing constitutional claims).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States Postal Service and federal parties argue that Konan’s suit is barred because it falls within FTCA limits/exceptions that preserve sovereign immunity and thus eliminate jurisdiction (i.e., Congress has not consented to this category of claim). They contend the Fifth Circuit incorrectly allowed the action to proceed despite the FTCA’s text and structure, and that expanding FTCA liability in this setting would improperly circumvent the statutory boundary lines Congress set for tort suits against the federal government.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Konan argues that her claim fits within the FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity and is not captured by the exceptions invoked by the government; the Fifth Circuit correctly treated the alleged conduct as actionable under the FTCA’s terms. Supporting amici emphasize that, given the narrowing of other remedies against federal officials, the Court should not construe FTCA exceptions broadly or out of context in a way that effectively leaves injured parties with no remedy and elevates federal officials above ordinary legal accountability.
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)
Burgo v. Parish of St. Tammany, 187 F.3d 452 (5th Cir. 1999)
Thornton v. Merchant, 526 F. App’x 385 (5th Cir. 2013)
Benningfield v. City of Houston, 157 F.3d 369 (5th Cir. 1998)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are right to press Dolan’s admonition against reading § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” and to worry that intentional, discriminatory withholding feels like an “independent wrong.” But the statutory line Congress drew withdraws the waiver for “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of postal matter, and—as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize—“negligent” modifies only “transmission,” leaving “loss” and “miscarriage” unqualified and naturally encompassing nondelivery whatever the motive. Accepting an intent-based carveout would make the same operative words do different work depending on culpability and invite artful “repackaging” of nondelivery claims to evade a carefully drawn exception defining the scope of consent to suit. Whatever remedial gap Westfall substitution may create, it is not a license for us to narrow § 2680(b) beyond its text and structural role in the FTCA’s waiver-plus-enumerated-exceptions scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the Dolan caution against pressing § 2680(b) to its “outer limits” and thereby creating an accountability gap for intentional, discriminatory withholding. But Dolan’s contextual narrowing cannot supply an intent limitation that the text lacks: “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” while “loss” and “miscarriage” are independent terms that naturally cover nondelivery, however caused, and this claim still “aris[es] out of” mail not being delivered, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize. Under the FTCA’s element-and-exception structure, § 1346(b)’s waiver is conditioned on the absence of a § 2680 exception; once § 2680(b) applies, the court may not proceed to remedial-gap concerns or state-law merits. Whatever policy concerns remain, they are for Congress to address by adjusting the scope of the postal-matter exception, not for us to rewrite it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is her Dolan-based contextual reading that § 2680(b) targets ordinary postal mishaps and not intentional, discriminatory withholding, and Justice Kagan’s related “remedial dead zone” concern is not trivial given Westfall substitution. But those arguments ultimately ask us to add a culpability limitation Congress did not write: as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” while “loss” and “miscarriage” stand on their own and naturally cover non-delivery regardless of intent. On these pleadings the injury still “aris[es] out of” the nondelivery/withholding of mail, and accepting respondent’s approach would invite artful pleading and the spillover effects Justice Roberts warns about—turning routine nondelivery disputes into FTCA damages actions whenever intent is alleged. Whatever accountability gap remains is a consequence of the FTCA’s enumerated exceptions and Congress’s chosen remedial channel, not something we are free to narrow by judicial construction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s textual point—that “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” leaving “loss” and “miscarriage” unqualified—carries real force, but it proves too much when read in statutory context. As Dolan cautioned, we should not drive § 2680(b) to its outer definitional limits; “loss” and “miscarriage,” paired with “negligent transmission,” most naturally capture the ordinary operational hazards of carrying and delivering mail, not an employee’s intentional, discriminatory withholding as an independent wrong. Justice Gorsuch’s concern about artful pleading is addressed by focusing on the gravamen: whether the challenged conduct is a routine failure of delivery or a deliberate diversion/sabotage divorced from postal “mishap.” Reading § 2680(b) to immunize intentional interference would transform a targeted postal-delivery exception into a sweeping shield for culpable misconduct—an expansion Congress did not clearly enact within the FTCA’s remedial scheme.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett press the hardest textual point: “negligent” most naturally modifies only “transmission,” and “loss”/“miscarriage” can linguistically cover nondelivery regardless of intent, with a risk of artful pleading. But Dolan’s warning against reading the postal exception to its “outer limits” matters because statutory terms take their meaning from context; here the trio—“loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission”—reads as a package aimed at the ordinary incidents of postal carriage and delivery, not intentional diversion or discriminatory withholding as an independent wrong. Treating deliberate sabotage as categorically within § 2680(b) would make a narrow carveout swallow the FTCA’s accountability baseline and create a practical remedial dead zone given Westfall substitution—an expansion Congress did not speak to with the clarity we ordinarily require for broad immunity. The more workable, coherent line is to ask whether the claim targets failures in the course of transmission and delivery (covered) or an employee’s intentional interference outside that ordinary operational risk (not covered), and on these allegations it is the latter.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan raise the hardest concern: Dolan’s caution against reading § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” and the prospect of an accountability gap if intentional, discriminatory withholding is treated the same as routine mishaps. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, Congress did not draft an intent-based limitation: “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” while “loss” and “miscarriage” stand on their own, and this suit still “aris[es] out of” mail that did not arrive. Accepting respondent’s “independent wrong” framing would make § 2680(b)’s application turn on pleading choices about mens rea, inviting an end-run around a categorical exception that defines the scope of the government’s consent to suit. Under the FTCA’s sequencing, once the postal-matter exception fits the gravamen of the claim, the waiver is clawed back and we should not reach state-law merits or remedial-gap policy arguments.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the best push by invoking Dolan’s warning against reading § 2680(b) to its “outer limits” and characterizing intentional, discriminatory withholding as an independent wrong. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the enacted text withdraws the FTCA waiver for “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of postal matter, and “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” not “loss” or “miscarriage,” so an intent-based carveout would add a limitation Congress did not write. The gravamen here is non-delivery/withholding of mail—injury flowing directly from mail not arriving—so the claim still “aris[es] out of” a loss or miscarriage within § 2680(b)’s categorical boundary. Any remedial gap created by Westfall substitution is a consequence of the statutory scheme, and—as Justice Roberts notes—is for Congress to fix rather than for us to narrow an immunity-preserving exception beyond its text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest case that Dolan counsels against reading § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” and that intentional, discriminatory withholding feels like an “independent wrong” rather than an ordinary postal mishap. But the statutory gatekeeping question is whether there exists a right to sue under the FTCA once the claim is properly characterized, and the text withdraws the waiver for “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of postal matter—terms that are not culpability-limited, with “negligent” modifying only “transmission,” as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize. Dolan’s narrowing move was about context and overbreadth at the margins, not about inserting an intent-based carveout Congress did not enact; treating intent as dispositive would make § 2680(b)’s application turn on pleading and undermine the waiver-plus-enumerated-exceptions architecture. Whatever remedial-gap concerns flow from Westfall substitution, they are downstream of the threshold statutory limit on consent to suit and cannot justify reworking § 2680(b)’s operative terms.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the best equitable and purposive point: Dolan warns against pushing § 2680(b) to its outer bounds, and it feels discordant to treat intentional, discriminatory withholding as just another “postal mishap.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the text Congress chose withdraws the waiver for “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of mail, and the most natural grammatical reading is that “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” leaving “loss” and “miscarriage” unqualified. In the FTCA’s structure—waiver in § 1346(b) cabined by categorical carveouts in § 2680—an intent-based carveout would make the exception’s operation hinge on culpability labels and pleading choices rather than the statutory category of injury (non-delivery). However troubling the remedial gap that the Westfall substitution regime may produce, I do not see a sufficiently clear textual hook to narrow an immunity-preserving exception beyond its ordinary meaning.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver is limited by the exceptions Congress enacted, and we read those exceptions in light of the statute’s text and overall remedial architecture rather than allowing artful “repackaging” of a mail-delivery dispute into a different tort label. On these facts—intentional interference with or withholding of mail by postal employees—the claim most naturally “aris[es] out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of postal matter within § 2680(b), which preserves immunity and therefore defeats subject-matter jurisdiction. Interpreting § 2680(b) to turn on whether the non-delivery was negligent or intentional would risk making the same operative words (“loss” and “miscarriage”) do different work depending on the theory of culpability, contrary to coherent statutory construction. Whatever the perceived remedial gap, it is for Congress—not the courts—to expand the FTCA’s consent to suit beyond the carefully delimited exceptions it chose.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver in § 1346(b) applies only if, under the “law of the place,” a similarly situated private person would be liable; but Congress simultaneously preserved sovereign immunity in § 2680(b) for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” On the facts alleged—intentional interference with delivery by postal employees—the gravamen of the suit is that mail failed to arrive (or arrived in the wrong manner), which fits within “loss” or “miscarriage,” terms not limited by the word “negligent,” and thus the exception restores immunity and deprives the federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction. Consistent with Arbaugh and Brownback, that conclusion follows from the statute’s elements/limitations: because the claim falls outside § 1346(b) by operation of an enumerated exception, the court is not reaching a freestanding “jurisdictional label” but applying Congress’s substantive boundary on the cause of action. The Fifth Circuit’s contrary approach effectively narrows § 2680(b) to negligence despite its text and Dolan’s focus on injuries arising because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or at the wrong address.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and under the Westfall Act it is the exclusive damages channel for torts committed by federal employees within the scope of employment; that makes the FTCA’s exceptions the controlling boundary lines for jurisdiction. On the facts alleged—postal employees intentionally diverting or withholding plaintiff’s mail—the injury still “arises out of” a failure in the delivery of postal matter, i.e., a “loss” or “miscarriage” within 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b), which preserves immunity for that category of claims. Dolan’s narrowing construction does not authorize courts to carve an intent-based exception into § 2680(b)’s text; once an exception applies, Congress has withheld consent to suit and the federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction. Expanding liability here would invite spillover by converting routine mail-delivery disputes into FTCA damages actions whenever a plaintiff pleads intentional misconduct, contrary to the statutory scheme Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Starting with the text and structure, § 2680(b) preserves immunity for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail; read in context, that phrasing most naturally targets ordinary postal failures in delivery and carriage, not a postal employee’s alleged intentional, discriminatory withholding of mail as an independent wrong. As in Dolan, I would resist stretching the postal exception “to the outer limits of its definitional possibilities,” especially where doing so would convert a narrow carveout into a broad shield for culpable malfeasance and leave injured parties without the accountability mechanism Congress created in the FTCA. Nor does the discretionary-function exception fit these alleged facts: intentional interference with delivery for improper reasons is operational wrongdoing, not the kind of policy judgment § 2680(a) is meant to protect. Because the claim plausibly falls within the FTCA’s waiver as a tort actionable under state-law analogues and is not clearly captured by an exception, I would affirm jurisdiction and allow the suit to proceed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: On the pleaded facts—intentional misconduct by postal employees that prevented delivery—the claim does not naturally fit § 2680(b)’s limited carveout for injuries “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, which is best read (for coherence and workability) to cover the ordinary operational failures of the postal system rather than intentional, wrongful acts. Dolan teaches that we should not treat the postal exception as a sweeping bar for anything connected to mail, but instead construe it in a way that preserves the FTCA’s general waiver where Congress has not clearly withdrawn it. Reading § 2680(b) to reach intentional diversion or sabotage would expand the exception beyond its text and undermine a workable remedial scheme—especially given the Westfall Act’s channeling of employee tort suits into the FTCA and the Court’s narrowing of other personal-liability remedies—without a clear congressional instruction to do so. Because the exception does not plainly cover this kind of intentional wrongdoing, jurisdiction remains under § 1346(b) and the suit may proceed against the United States/USPS.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Starting with § 1346(b)(1), Konan alleges tortious acts by postal employees within the scope of employment, but that waiver applies only insofar as no § 2680 exception withdraws it. Here the gravamen of the complaint is injury “arising out of” mail that failed to arrive because USPS employees allegedly refused to deliver it—squarely within § 2680(b)’s retention of immunity for claims arising from “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter, terms that are not limited to negligence. Under Dolan, the postal exception covers injuries caused directly or consequentially by mail failing to arrive (even if the pleaded misconduct is intentional), so the exception “claws back” the waiver and deprives the court of subject-matter jurisdiction before any state-law merits inquiry. Because Congress has preserved immunity for this category of postal non-delivery claims, the suit cannot proceed against the United States/USPS under the FTCA.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Start with the statute’s words and scheme. Section 2680(b) withdraws the FTCA’s waiver for “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of letters or postal matter,” and on these facts the gravamen of Konan’s damages claim is the non-delivery/withholding of her mail—i.e., a claim that arises out of a “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter even if the underlying conduct is alleged to be intentional. Read in context of § 1346(b)(1)’s limited waiver and § 2680’s enumerated exceptions, that exception preserves sovereign immunity and therefore strips the federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction over this category of claim. The Westfall Act’s substitution/exclusivity rules reinforce that Congress channeled employee tort claims into the FTCA only to the extent the United States has consented to suit; when an FTCA exception applies, plaintiffs cannot repackage the same injury as a tort claim against the United States/USPS for damages.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by § 2680’s exceptions, and those exceptions operate as threshold, jurisdictional gatekeepers: if the claim falls within an exception, the plaintiff lacks a right to sue the United States and the court cannot reach the merits. On the alleged facts—postal employees intentionally refusing to deliver or deliberately interfering with the delivery of plaintiff’s mail—the claim “aris[es] out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of postal matter within the ordinary meaning of those terms, with “negligent” modifying only “transmission” and not narrowing “loss” or “miscarriage” to accidental conduct. Read in the FTCA’s overall structure (waiver in § 1346(b) bounded by categorical carveouts in § 2680), the postal exception preserves immunity even when the delivery failure is alleged to be intentional, so subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking. Remedies-based concerns cannot overcome the statute’s text; Congress chose to withhold consent for this class of mail-delivery claims, even if other avenues (e.g., non-FTCA claims not barred by substitution, or administrative/criminal processes) may be limited.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying a whole-text and whole-statute approach to the FTCA, the waiver in § 1346(b) is expressly limited by § 2680’s categorical carveouts, which function to preserve sovereign immunity (and thus defeat jurisdiction) for claims Congress chose not to allow. On these facts—alleged intentional interference with the handling/delivery of mail by postal employees—the claim most naturally “aris[es] out of” a postal failure that Congress addressed in the postal-matter exception, § 2680(b), and respondent’s effort to recharacterize that conduct to escape the exception reads the statute in a strained, acontextual way. Dolan underscores that § 2680(b) marks a line between actionable postal torts and retained immunity, and that line is drawn by the terms “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” as they operate within the FTCA’s carefully bounded remedial scheme; where Congress has retained immunity for mail-handling harms, courts should not expand liability by clever relabeling. That is especially so because the FTCA’s design couples waiver with enumerated exceptions, and the existence of other remedial/administrative avenues for mail-related injuries confirms § 2680(b)’s role as a boundary-setting provision rather than a gap to be judicially narrowed.
